question: Is either of these true: the 2024 return these figures come from was a joint return, and for 2025 you are not filing a joint return with the same spouse (for example after a divorce, a separation or the death of your spouse in 2024); or, on this 2025 joint return, you and your spouse each filed a separate 2024 return whose Schedule D line 21 showed a loss?

findings.situation: A filer who filed jointly for 2024 and not jointly with that spouse for 2025 (for example, after a divorce) has no 2024 capital loss carryover because the 2024 Schedule D line 21 was not a loss, yet must answer YES and is refused.
findings.irs_text: Question: "the 2024 return these figures come from was a joint return, and for 2025 you are not filing a joint return with the same spouse". i1040sd p. 10: "if your 2024 Schedule D, line 21, is a loss and... Otherwise, you don't have any carryovers."
findings.why: The first limb has no loss or carryover condition, unlike the second limb, so it catches filers with nothing to allocate. The tool correctly computes a zero carryover for them, and the spouse-allocation rule has no effect.

findings.situation: A filer who filed jointly for 2024 and not jointly with that spouse for 2025 actually had the entire loss behind the joint carryover, yet must answer YES and is refused.
findings.irs_text: Question: "the 2024 return these figures come from was a joint return, and for 2025 you are not filing a joint return with the same spouse". i1040sd p. 10: "any capital loss carryover from the joint return can be deducted only on the return of the spouse who actually had the loss."
findings.why: When all of the loss belongs to the filer, the whole carryover figured from the joint return's amounts is deductible on the filer's return, so no allocation is needed. The worksheet computation is therefore correct, but the question's wording still forces a refusal.

question: Does the special rule for children of divorced or separated parents, or parents who lived apart (including parents who never married), apply to this person, for example because a Form 8332 release or a decree lets the noncustodial parent claim the child? Answer yes whether you are the custodial parent who signed the release (or whose decree or agreement lets the other parent claim the child) or the noncustodial parent using it. A release the custodial parent has revoked still applies for 2025 unless written notice of the revocation was given (or reasonable efforts were made to give it) to the noncustodial parent in 2024 or earlier.

findings.situation: A custodial parent's post-2008 divorce decree says the noncustodial parent may claim the child, but the custodial parent never signed Form 8332 or a similar statement, so the special rule does not apply and the custodial parent's qualifying-child result is computed correctly.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 20: "If the divorce decree or separation agreement went into effect after 2008, the noncustodial parent can't include pages from the decree or agreement instead of Form 8332. The custodial parent must sign either Form 8332 or a substantially similar statement"
findings.why: The question tells the filer to answer yes if they are the custodial parent "whose decree or agreement lets the other parent claim the child." A post-2008 decree alone does not satisfy condition 4, so this filer is refused even though the tool would compute their case correctly.

findings.situation: A pre-1985 decree lets the noncustodial parent claim the child, but that parent provided less than $600 of support in 2025, so the rule does not apply and the custodial parent keeps the child.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 20: "A pre-1985 decree ... provides that the noncustodial parent can claim the child as a dependent, and the noncustodial parent provides at least $600 for support of the child during 2025."
findings.why: The question's wording ("a decree lets the noncustodial parent claim the child") leads to yes without the $600 support condition, so a case the tool computes correctly is refused.

findings.situation: A custodial parent signed a Form 8332 release that covers only alternate years (for example 2024 and 2026), not 2025.
findings.irs_text: p501 p. 22: "The release can be for 1 year, for a number of specified years (for example, alternate years), or for all future years, as specified in the declaration."
findings.why: The question asks about "a Form 8332 release" that "lets the noncustodial parent claim the child" without saying it must cover 2025. The filer could answer yes even though, for 2025, the custodial parent's case is computed correctly.

findings.situation: Divorced or never-married parents lived apart, and no release or qualifying decree exists, so the custodial parent claims the child under the ordinary rules.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 20: "A child will be treated as the qualifying child or qualifying relative of the child's noncustodial parent (defined later) if all of the following conditions apply."
findings.why: The question asks whether "the special rule for children of divorced or separated parents, or parents who lived apart" applies, and gives a release only as an example. A divorced custodial parent could read the rule as applying just because the parents are divorced and live apart, and answer yes.

question: Is this person a child who, at any time during 2025, was presumed by law enforcement authorities to have been kidnapped by someone who isn't a member of your family or the child's family (even if the child has since been returned)?

findings.situation: A child disappeared in mid-2025, but law enforcement did not presume a non-family kidnapping until early 2026, before the return was filed, so the months-lived count could fall to 6 or fewer.
findings.irs_text: "The child is presumed by law enforcement authorities to have been kidnapped by someone who isn't a member of your family or the child's family." (p501, 2025, p. 13); "In the year the kidnapping occurred, the child lived with you for more than half of the part of the year before the date of the kidnapping." (p501, 2025, p. 13)
findings.why: The IRS text ties the year to when the kidnapping occurred and sets no deadline for the presumption, but the question asks whether the child was presumed kidnapped "at any time during 2025." This filer could truthfully answer NO, and the tool would then compute the residency lines as false even though the kidnapped-child treatment may apply.

findings.situation: A child was presumed kidnapped for a few days in 2025, was returned, and lived with the filer for well over six months anyway.
findings.irs_text: Question: "at any time during 2025, was presumed by law enforcement authorities to have been kidnapped ... (even if the child has since been returned)"; IRS: "To meet this test, your child must have lived with you for more than half the year." (p501, 2025, p. 13)
findings.why: The filer must answer YES, but the child meets the residency test on actual time lived, so the months count gives the correct result. The tool refuses a case it computes correctly.

findings.situation: A child was presumed kidnapped during 2025 but did not live with the filer for more than half of the part of the year before the kidnapping, or for more than half of the part of the year after the child's return.
findings.irs_text: Question: "Is this person a child who, at any time during 2025, was presumed by law enforcement authorities to have been kidnapped"; IRS: "You can treat your child as meeting the residency test even if the child has been kidnapped, but the following statements must be true." followed by statements 2 and 3 on time lived before the kidnapping and after the return (p501, 2025, p. 13)
findings.why: The question tests only statement 1, so the filer answers YES even though the special treatment is unavailable. The ordinary months count, which the tool computes, would correctly apply if the child also fell short of more than half the year.

findings.situation: A child still presumed kidnapped during 2025 is past the end of the special treatment because the child would have reached age 18, or there was a determination of death, in an earlier year.
findings.irs_text: Question: "at any time during 2025, was presumed by law enforcement authorities to have been kidnapped"; IRS: "This treatment applies for all years until the earlier of: 1. The year there is a determination that the child is dead, or 2. The year the child would have reached age 18." (p501, 2025, p. 13)
findings.why: The question has no age or death cutoff, so a filer with a continuing presumption answers YES after the treatment has ended. The ordinary months count would correctly decide these lines, so the refusal is unnecessary.

findings.situation: The person presumed kidnapped was 18 or older, or was a relative such as a sibling, niece, or nephew rather than the filer's own child.
findings.irs_text: Question: "Is this person a child"; IRS: "You can treat your child as meeting the residency test even if the child has been kidnapped" (p501, 2025, p. 13); "To meet this test, a child must be: Your son, daughter, stepchild, or foster child, or a descendant ... Your brother, sister, half brother, half sister, stepbrother, or stepsister, or a descendant" (p501, 2025, p. 13)
findings.why: "A child" could mean a minor, the filer's own offspring, or anyone who fits the qualifying-child relationship test. Filers in the same situation could therefore answer differently, and the question does not say which meaning applies.

question: Was this person married at the end of 2025 (a person legally separated under a decree of divorce or separate maintenance is not married), or is a joint return being filed for 2025 that includes this person (including one filed by this person with a spouse who died during 2025, or by this person's surviving spouse after this person died during 2025)?

findings.situation: The person was married at the end of 2025 but neither files a joint return nor files one only to claim a refund, so the Step 1 and Step 4 tests, which the tool computes, apply to this person unchanged.
findings.irs_text: Question: "Was this person married at the end of 2025 ...?"; i1040gi p. 21: "if the person is married but doesn't file a joint return or files a joint return only to claim a refund of withheld income tax or estimated tax paid, you may be able to claim that person as a dependent ... go to Step 2, question 3 ... or Step 4, question 4"
findings.why: Marriage is not one of the conditions in Step 1 (p. 17) or Step 4 (p. 19). Marriage matters only at Step 2, question 2 and Step 4, question 3, after these lines are decided, so the qualifying_child and qualifying_relative computations are correct for this person but the question forces YES. The EIC line does need the refusal, because the Married child rule (p. 44) makes EIC status depend on dependency.

findings.situation: The person's spouse died during 2025, so the person was not married at year end, and a joint return is filed only to claim a refund of withholding.

findings.why: The tool's helper "Included on a 2025 joint return filed other than only to claim a refund?" = false is correct for a joint return filed only for a refund. The EIC Married child rule does not reach a person who was unmarried at year end. The question still forces YES for any joint return.

question: Did you and others together provide over half of this person's support for 2025, with no one person providing over half (a multiple support situation), whether you or another contributor claims the person?

findings.situation: The filer is one of several contributors in a multiple support situation, but another contributor claims the person, so the filer cannot claim the person; the tool already computes this correctly as not a qualifying relative because the filer did not provide over half.
findings.irs_text: Question: "...with no one person providing over half (a multiple support situation), whether you or another contributor claims the person?" i1040gi p. 19: "For whom you provided over half of the person's support in 2025."
findings.why: The clause "whether you or another contributor claims the person" makes this filer answer YES and get refused. Yet the computed line already gives the right result here: the support helper is false, so there is no qualifying relative for this filer.

findings.situation: Several people together provided over half the support, but the filer cannot be treated as providing over half (for example, the filer's own contribution is too small, or the other contributors could not claim the person anyway), so the tool's 'not a qualifying relative' result is correct.

findings.why: The question asks only whether the combined contributions passed half with no single person over half. The IRS rule says the special treatment only "may apply," so filers it can never help still answer YES and are refused.

question: Does this person meet the conditions to be the qualifying child of any other person for 2025, under the dependent rules or under the EIC rules (which have no support test)?

findings.situation: A custodial parent has released the claim to the child on Form 8332, and the noncustodial parent, with whom the child did not live for more than half of 2025, claims the child.
findings.irs_text: "A child will be treated as the qualifying child or qualifying relative of the child's noncustodial parent... only the noncustodial parent can claim the child for purposes of the child tax credit and credit for other dependents" (i1040gi 2025, p. 20); see also "unless the special rule for Children of divorced or separated parents... applies" (p. 21).
findings.why: The noncustodial parent fails the lived-with test and is only treated as having a qualifying child, so the custodial filer can truthfully answer NO to "meet the conditions." The tool then computes dependent.qualifying_child as true for a filer who has released the claim, and the question also does not catch a noncustodial filer whose line computes false on the lived-with helper.

findings.situation: A child who was married at the end of 2025 and is not filing a joint return lives with the filer, but the filer cannot claim the child as a dependent and the divorced-or-separated-parents exception does not apply.
findings.irs_text: "If the child was married, see Married child, later" (i1040gi 2025, p. 41); "A child who was married at the end of 2025 is a qualifying child only if (a) you can claim the child as your dependent, or (b) you could have claimed the child as your dependent except for the special rule for Children of divorced or separated parents" (p. 44).
findings.why: The question asks only about other people's claims, so a filer can truthfully answer NO when no one else qualifies. The computed dependent.eic_child has no married-child condition and returns true for a child the text excludes.

findings.situation: The child lives with the filer and another person and provided over half of their own support, so the child fails the support test for dependent.qualifying_child but meets the EIC conditions for the other person.
findings.irs_text: Question: "under the dependent rules or under the EIC rules (which have no support test)"; IRS: "Who didn't provide over half of their own support for 2025" (i1040gi 2025, p. 17).
findings.why: The EIC branch forces YES, which also refuses dependent.qualifying_child. That line would correctly compute false from the support helper without any tie-breaker, because the child is not a dependent-rule qualifying child of anyone.

findings.situation: The filer is the child's only parent among the eligible claimants, such as a parent living with the child and the filer's own parent, so the tie-breaker necessarily resolves in the filer's favor.
findings.irs_text: Question: "Does this person meet the conditions to be the qualifying child of any other person for 2025"; IRS: "If only one of the persons is the child's parent, the child is treated as the qualifying child of the parent" and "you can claim Lee as a qualifying child" (i1040gi 2025, pp. 21, 44).
findings.why: The filer must truthfully answer YES and is refused, although the tool's computed true result is the correct outcome. This over-refusal is conservative, but it does block a case the tool computes correctly.

findings.situation: Another person meets the qualifying-child tests on paper but will not or need not claim the child, for example because that person is not filing or is filing only for a refund.
findings.irs_text: "Even if a child meets the conditions to be the qualifying child of more than one person" and "If you and any other person can claim the child as a qualifying child" (i1040gi 2025, p. 21); compare "Check 'No' if the other person isn't required to file, and isn't filing" (p. 41, Step 3, question 6).
findings.why: A filer could read "meet the conditions" as covering only the listed relationship, age, joint-return, residency and support tests, and answer YES. A filer could also read it as requiring someone who can actually claim the child, by analogy to the non-filer carve-out on p. 41, and answer NO.

question: Were you (or your spouse, if filing jointly) covered in 2025 by two or more dependent care plans that allow different maximum amounts to be excluded?

findings.situation: A filer is covered by two plans that each allow the same maximum below $5,000 (for example, $3,000 each, under two employers), so they truthfully answer NO and the tool enters $3,000 on line 21.
findings.irs_text: i2441 (2025) p. 5, Line 21: "Enter on line 21 the maximum amount that you may exclude for the year under your dependent care plan" and "Don't enter more than the maximum amount allowed under your dependent care plan."
findings.why: The text speaks of one plan's maximum, so it does not settle whether same-maximum plans use the single-plan amount or a combined amount up to the $5,000 limit. This is the same gap the refusal gives for differing maximums, but the question's "different maximum amounts" wording lets this case through to a computed $3,000.

findings.situation: A filer is eligible for or enrolled in two plans with different maximums but received benefits under only one, and could answer YES or NO depending on how they read "covered."

findings.why: "Covered" could mean merely eligible, enrolled, or actually receiving benefits, while the IRS text ties line 21 to the amount the filer may exclude under their plan. The same facts could therefore lead to either a refusal or a computation using the one plan's maximum.

question: In 2025, were you (or your spouse, if filing jointly) a full-time student at a school for some part of each of 5 calendar months, or physically or mentally not able to care for yourself at any time? (This includes paying for the care of your spouse who was not able to care for themselves.)

findings.situation: An unmarried filer (single or head of household) who was a full-time student or unable to care for themselves must answer YES and is refused, even though deemed income appears to be available only on a joint return, so the tool's actual earned income would be correct.
findings.irs_text: p503 (2025) p. 11: 'These rules also apply if you are a student or not able to care for yourself and are filing a joint return.' Compare i2441 (2025) p. 4: 'These rules for a spouse who was a student or disabled also apply to you if you were a student or disabled.'
findings.why: The question asks 'were you ... a full-time student ... or physically or mentally not able to care for yourself' without regard to filing status. Pub. 503 limits the filer's own deemed income to joint returns, although i2441 p. 4 states no such limit, so this finding depends on following Pub. 503.

findings.situation: A filer who was a student or unable to care for themselves, and whose actual earned income met or exceeded the $250 or $500 floor in every such month, must answer YES although deemed income would not change lines 4 or 18.
findings.irs_text: i2441 (2025) p. 4: 'If you also worked during that month, enter the higher of $250 (or $500) or your actual earned income for that month.'
findings.why: The question asks only about status ('were you ... a full-time student ... or ... not able to care for yourself'), not whether the floor raises income in any month. Where actual earnings are the higher figure every month, the tool's sum of actual earned income is the correct result.

findings.situation: A filer enrolled full-time for 5 or more months only in a correspondence school, an internet-only school, or an on-the-job training course can truthfully answer YES and is refused, although that enrollment does not qualify for deemed income.
findings.irs_text: i2441 (2025) p. 4: 'A school doesn't include an on-the-job training course, a correspondence school, or a school offering courses only through the Internet.'
findings.why: The question says 'a full-time student at a school' and does not give this exclusion, so an ordinary reading of 'school' includes these programs. Without deemed income, the tool's actual earned income is correct for this filer.

findings.situation: A filer with a temporary illness or injury, or a disability that did not prevent self-care, could reasonably answer either way to 'physically or mentally not able to care for yourself at any time'.
findings.irs_text: i2441 (2025) p. 1: 'Persons who can't dress, clean, or feed themselves because of physical or mental disabilities are considered not able to care for themselves. Also, persons who must have constant attention to prevent them from injuring themselves or others are considered not able to care for themselves.'
findings.why: The question omits the IRS test, and 'not able to care for yourself at any time' could be read to include short periods of needing help. A filer who reads it loosely may be refused unnecessarily, while one who reads it strictly may answer NO despite meeting the IRS test.

Include investment expenses incurred directly by you or reported to you on Schedule K-1 from a partnership, or by an S corporation..."

findings.situation: A filer with other deductible investment expenses answers NO, and the filing-exception helper may treat them as exempt from filing even though the exception requires having no such expenses.

findings.situation: A filer who elects on line 4g to include qualified dividends in investment income, often with no line 4e net capital gain, may read the question as asking whether they are electing to treat qualified dividends as investment income, and answer YES.

findings.why: The wording "allocation of line 4g to qualified dividends" can be read as the ordinary line 4g election, which the tool computes, rather than the separate "Elec." election on line 4e. Under that reading the filer answers YES and the tool refuses lines it handles correctly.

findings.situation: A filer counts capitalized interest (section 263A) or section 264 interest on debt tied to life insurance or annuity contracts as investment interest, including in a 2024 carryforward, and truthfully answers NO.

findings.situation: A filer whose Schedule K-1 reports portfolio investment expenses (section 212 expenses that are nondeductible miscellaneous itemized deductions in 2025) answers YES because of the K-1 example, although line 5 is correctly zero.

findings.why: The question's example "investment expenses on a Schedule K-1" brings in K-1 expenses that are not allowed deductions, so the tool's zero for line 5 would have been right.

findings.situation: A filer who pays investment advisory fees, or has depreciation on a passive rental, cannot tell whether that is a "deductible investment expense other than interest".
findings.irs_text: f4952 p. 4, Line 5: "Investment expenses don't include any deductions used in determining your income or loss from a passive activity. Don't include any miscellaneous itemized deductions..."
findings.why: The question does not say that passive-activity deductions and nondeductible miscellaneous expenses are excluded. A filer could answer YES, which is wide, or NO, which is correct.

findings.situation: A filer with mutual fund capital gain distributions, capital loss carryovers or annuity income cannot tell whether these are "other investment income or expense beyond interest, dividends and securities sales".

findings.why: Capital gain distributions and carryovers are not literally securities sales, and annuities are not named. Some filers would answer YES even though none of these change lines 2, 5, the election or the filing test.

question:
Does any of these apply?

- someone enrolled in a Marketplace policy was not lawfully present in the United States
- for any month, anyone in your tax family was eligible for minimum essential coverage other than coverage in the individual market, including:
  - Medicare Part A or Part C
  - Medicaid
  - the Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP)
  - TRICARE
  - certain benefits for veterans and their families
  - health coverage for Peace Corps volunteers
  - employer-sponsored coverage that was offered and was affordable and provided minimum value (other than during a waiting period before the benefits begin; the offer is affordable for the employee if the employee's share of the annual cost of self-only coverage is not more than 9.02% of household income (Form 8962, line 3), whatever family coverage costs, and for another member of the tax family allowed to enroll if the employee's share of the annual cost of coverage for the employee and the family members allowed to enroll is not more than 9.02% of household income)
  - employer-sponsored coverage the person actually enrolled in (including COBRA or retiree coverage) even if it was not affordable or did not provide minimum value
  - other health coverage the Department of Health and Human Services designates as minimum essential coverage
- you or a family member were offered or covered by a qualified small employer HRA (QSEHRA, W-2 box 12 code FF) or an individual coverage HRA for 2025
- any part of a month's premium was not paid by the due date of your return, not including extensions (or, for coverage you enrolled in retroactively after a successful eligibility appeal, by the 120th day after the appeals decision), or a Form 1095-A shows zero in column A for a month whose premium you paid

  - similar items: items of the same general category or type, such as coin collections, paintings, books, clothing, jewelry, nonpublicly traded stock, land or buildings
  - publicly traded securities: listed on a recognized stock exchange whose quotations are published daily, regularly traded on a national or regional over-the-counter market, or mutual fund shares quoted daily in a national newspaper

findings.situation: A filer gives more than $5,000 of securities that are not publicly traded in the listed sense but qualify under Regulations section 1.170A-13(c)(7)(xi)(B), so they belong in Section A and need no appraisal. The question still makes the filer answer YES.
findings.irs_text: i8283 p.3: 'The following items even if the claimed value was more than $5,000 ... d. Certain other securities even though the securities do not meet any of the criteria described in paragraphs 2.a through 2.c above (for more information, see Regulations section 1.170A-13(c)(7)(xi)(B))'
findings.why: The question exempts only 'publicly traded securities' as it defines them. These Section A securities fall outside that definition, so the tool refuses a gift it could compute as a normal Section A amount.

findings.situation: Property is worth more than $5,000, but the required reductions bring the deduction to $5,000 or less. Examples are ordinary income property limited to basis, or capital gain property reduced to basis.
findings.irs_text: i8283 p.3: 'Include in Section B only items (or groups of similar items) for which you claimed a deduction of more than $5,000' versus 'A separate, qualified appraisal is required for any gift of property valued in excess of $5,000'; i8283 p.1: 'Make any required reductions to the amount of the contributions before you determine if you must file Form 8283.'
findings.why: The question says 'a deduction over $5,000 (before any income limit), or property worth more than $5,000' and never says the deduction test comes after the required reductions. A filer cannot tell whether a reduced deduction of $5,000 or less still means YES, and the IRS text itself points both ways.

findings.situation: A filer donates a partial interest or property with use restrictions, and the deduction is $5,000 or less. The question's list covers 'conservation or partial interests' and 'property with restrictions on its use' with no dollar threshold, so the filer answers YES.
findings.irs_text: i8283 p.3: 'You must also file Form 8283, Section B, if conditions were placed on the use of the property or you gave less than an entire interest in a property and the contribution was for more than $5,000.'
findings.why: The IRS requires Section B special treatment for these gifts only above $5,000. The question's blanket wording sweeps in smaller gifts that are ordinary Section A items. question: Was your earned income credit for any year after 1996, or your child tax credit, additional child tax credit or credit for other dependents for any year after 2015, reduced or disallowed for any reason other than a math or clerical error, or are you in a 2- or 10-year period during which you can't take one of these credits because an earlier claim was found to be reckless, intentional or fraudulent?

findings.situation: A filer's EIC was disallowed in an earlier year, but the filer later filed Form 8862, the EIC was allowed for that year, and it has not been reduced or disallowed again, so the filer must answer YES although no Form 8862 is needed for 2025.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 43: "But don’t file Form 8862 if either of the following applies. • You filed Form 8862 for another year, the EIC was allowed for that year, and your EIC hasn’t been reduced or disallowed again for any reason other than a math or clerical error."
findings.why: The question asks only whether the credit "for any year after 1996" was "reduced or disallowed" and has no carve-out for a later successful recertification. The tool's computation would be correct for this filer because the IRS text requires no Form 8862.

findings.situation: A filer is taking the EIC without a qualifying child, and the only reason an earlier EIC was reduced or disallowed was that a child on Schedule EIC was found not to be a qualifying child.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 43: "You are taking the EIC without a qualifying child and the only reason your EIC was reduced or disallowed in the other year was because it was determined that a child listed on Schedule EIC wasn’t your qualifying child."
findings.why: The question's phrase "reduced or disallowed for any reason other than a math or clerical error" requires YES, but the IRS text says not to file Form 8862 here. The tool would refuse a credit it can compute correctly.

findings.situation: A filer's CTC, ACTC or ODC was denied or reduced in an earlier year, but the filer filed Form 8862 for 2024 and the credit was allowed for that year, or another exception applies.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 39: "Don’t file Form 8862 if you filed Form 8862 for 2024, and the child tax credit, additional child tax credit, or credit for other dependents was allowed for that year." i1040s8812 p. 2: "you must attach Form 8862 to your tax return to claim the CTC, ACTC, or ODC unless an exception applies."
findings.why: The question has no exception for an earlier recertification, so this filer must answer YES. The IRS text does not require Form 8862 for this filer, so the tool's computation would be correct.

findings.situation: A filer has a past reduction, disallowance or ban affecting only one credit family, such as the EIC, and claims only the other family, such as the CTC, yet the single answer refuses both lines.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 43: "You must file Form 8862 if your EIC for a year after 1996 was reduced or disallowed" and "10 years after the most recent tax year for which there was a final determination that your EIC claim was due to fraud." i1040s8812 p. 2: "If your CTC, ACTC, or ODC for a year after 2015 was denied or reduced ... you must attach Form 8862 ... to claim the CTC, ACTC, or ODC" and "you will not be allowed to claim any of these credits for 10 years."
findings.why: The question joins both families with "or" and refers to "one of these credits," so a history with either family produces YES and refuses both lines. The quoted IRS text ties each Form 8862 requirement and ban to its own credit family, so the unaffected line would compute correctly.

findings.situation: A filer's earlier CTC or ODC was limited only by the income phase-out or by tax liability, and the IRS never denied or adjusted the claim.
findings.irs_text: i1040s8812 p. 2: "The maximum credit amount of your CTC and ODC may be reduced if either (1) or (2) applies." Compare: "If your CTC, ACTC, or ODC for a year after 2015 was denied or reduced for any reason other than a math or clerical error, you must attach Form 8862."
findings.why: The question's "reduced ... for any reason" does not say the reduction must be an IRS action on a claim, and the instructions also use "reduced" for the ordinary limits. question:
Does any of these apply to alimony you received or paid?

- payments under more than one divorce or separation agreement, or paid to more than one person
- a recapture of alimony (payments that decreased or ended during the first 3 calendar years, Pub. 504 Worksheet 1)
- payments of which part is not alimony:
  - child support (including payments that fell short of the total of child support and alimony required, and an amount the instrument reduces on a contingency relating to a child, such as reaching a certain age, or at a time associated with one)
  - payments for a home either of you owns (mortgage, real estate taxes, insurance, repairs; Pub. 504 Table 4)
  - payments of which any part must continue, in cash or property, for any period after the recipient spouse's death (even if the instrument does not say so, for example under state law), or payments for which a payment due after the death is a substitute

findings.situation: A pre-2019 agreement was modified after 2018 and the modification expressly adopts the post-2018 rules. Payments made after the modification are neither income nor deductible, but the filer answers NO and enters the full year's payments under the helper, which asks only whether the agreement was 'entered into on or before December 31, 2018'.
findings.irs_text: p504 p. 16: 'The alimony payments made in January 2025 through May 2025 are includible ... The alimony payments made in June 2025 through December 2025 are neither includible ... nor deductible'; i1040gi p. 89: 'unless that agreement was changed after December 31, 2018, to expressly provide that alimony received isn't included in your income'
findings.why: The question does not ask about modifications after 2018. A filer with one agreement and no recapture, child support, home payments or death contingency truthfully answers NO, and the tool computes the full amount even though part or all of it should be excluded.

findings.situation: Part of the payments is not alimony because it is a noncash property settlement, the recipient's share of community income, or upkeep of the payer's property other than a home, such as a car. The filer answers NO because the list names only child support, home payments and death-contingent payments.
findings.irs_text: p504 p. 13: 'Alimony doesn't include: • Child support, • Noncash property settlements, • Payments that are your spouse's part of community income ..., • Payments to keep up the payer's property, or • Use of the payer's property.'
findings.why: The heading 'payments of which part is not alimony' lists only some of the Pub. 504 exclusions, so a filer can read the list as complete. A filer who answers NO then has mixed payments computed as all alimony.

findings.situation: The payer pays the mortgage, real estate taxes or insurance on a home that only the recipient spouse owns. These payments are fully alimony and the tool computes them correctly, but the question's wording makes the filer answer YES.
findings.irs_text: p504 p. 13, Payments to a third party, Example 2: 'you must pay the real estate taxes and mortgage payments on a home owned by your spouse. If they otherwise qualify, you can deduct the payments as alimony'
findings.question_text: payments for a home either of you owns (mortgage, real estate taxes, insurance, repairs; Pub. 504 Table 4)
findings.why: 'Either of you owns' includes a home owned only by the recipient, where nothing needs to be split out. Only a home the payer owns, alone or jointly, needs the Table 4 or non-alimony treatment.

findings.situation: Payments decreased or ended during the first 3 calendar years, but no recapture applies. For example, the decrease is $15,000 or less from year 2 to year 3, it was caused by death or remarriage, it occurred under a temporary order, or it reflects a fixed share of income. findings.question_text: a recapture of alimony (payments that decreased or ended during the first 3 calendar years ...)
findings.why: The question does not say that the third year must be 2025. A filer could reasonably answer YES or NO for a recapture year that has already passed.

Does any of these apply to a canceled debt?

- it was canceled in a bankruptcy case or while you were insolvent, or is otherwise excluded from income (Form 982, for example qualified principal residence indebtedness)
- it was a student loan, was canceled as a gift or inheritance, was a reduction of the price of property you bought from the seller, or was owed to a corporation in which you hold stock

- it was canceled in connection with a foreclosure, repossession or abandonment of property (Form 1099-C box 7, or a Form 1099-A)
- it includes interest (Form 1099-C box 3) or any other amount (for example an unpaid medical bill) that would have been deductible if you had paid it

findings.situation: A filer has a canceled personal credit card or personal loan debt whose Form 1099-C shows nondeductible personal interest in box 3. The question's wording makes them answer YES, although the full box 2 amount is taxable and the tool computes it correctly.
findings.irs_text: Question: "it includes interest (Form 1099-C box 3) or any other amount ... that would have been deductible if you had paid it"; p525 p. 20: "If the interest would not be deductible (such as interest on a personal loan), include in your income the amount from box 2 of Form 1099-C."
findings.why: Read literally, the bullet triggers on any box 3 amount, but only deductible interest changes the result. Personal credit card interest is nondeductible, so it is fully covered by the computed line.

findings.situation: A filer whose debts exceed their assets only if retirement accounts and pension interests are left out could believe they were insolvent when they were not, or misjudge when insolvency is measured.
findings.irs_text: p4681 p. 6: "You were insolvent immediately before the cancellation to the extent that the total of all of your liabilities was more than the FMV of all of your assets ... assets include ... exempt assets ... such as your interest in a pension plan and the value of your retirement account"
findings.why: The question says "while you were insolvent" without the IRS definition or the "immediately before the cancellation" timing. A layperson could answer YES when the debt is fully taxable, or NO when part of it is excludable.

findings.situation: A filer whose Form 1099-C has box 5 checked may read the "(box 5)" reference as a cue to answer YES to "you were not personally liable for it."
findings.irs_text: p4681 p. 3: "Debt for which you are personally liable is recourse debt. All other debt is nonrecourse debt."
findings.why: On Form 1099-C, a checked box 5 means the debtor WAS personally liable. The parenthetical does not say whether a checked or unchecked box corresponds to YES, so the filer could answer it backwards in either direction.

findings.situation: A filer received a Form 1099-INT that includes interest received as a nominee (or accrued interest paid on a bond purchase), has no foreign accounts, and so truthfully answers NO; the tool then puts the gross roster total on line 2 without the required subtraction.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p.1: "Below this subtotal, enter 'Nominee Distribution' and show the total interest you received as a nominee. Subtract this amount from the subtotal and enter the result on line 2." p.2: "follow the rules earlier under Nominees ... identify the amount to be subtracted as 'Accrued Interest.'"
findings.why: Line 2 computes only the sum of interest.amount, but the IRS text requires subtracting nominee, accrued-interest, OID and ABP adjustments. FBAR status has nothing to do with these adjustments, so the screen never catches them.

findings.situation: A filer cashed post-1989 series EE or I bonds and paid qualified higher education expenses, has no foreign accounts, and so answers NO; line 3 is then forced to zero.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p.2, Line 3: "If, during 2025, you cashed series EE or I U.S. savings bonds issued after 1989 and you paid qualified higher education expenses ... you may be able to exclude part or all of the interest on those bonds. See Form 8815"
findings.why: Line 3 is hard-coded to zero, and the FBAR question gives a filer entitled to the Form 8815 exclusion no reason to answer YES.

findings.situation: A filer received a Form 1099-DIV that includes ordinary dividends received as a nominee, has no foreign accounts, and so answers NO; line 6 then takes box 1a gross.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p.2, Line 5 Nominees: "Below this subtotal, enter 'Nominee Distribution' and show the total ordinary dividends you received as a nominee. Subtract this amount from the subtotal and enter the result on line 6."
findings.why: Line 6 copies box 1a with no nominee subtraction, and FBAR status does not bring this situation to light.

findings.situation: A filer who must file an FBAR (foreign accounts above $10,000 in aggregate) but has only ordinary Form 1099-INT/1099-DIV amounts with no adjustments answers YES, and lines 2, 3 and 6 are refused even though the tool would compute them correctly.
findings.irs_text: Question: "Are you required to file FinCEN Form 114 (FBAR)?" i1040sb p.3: "A U.S. person that has a financial interest in or signature authority over foreign financial accounts must file the form if the aggregate value of foreign financial accounts exceeds $10,000"
findings.why: The FBAR requirement affects Part III (lines 7a/7b), not the interest and dividend amounts on lines 2, 3 and 6. A YES answer therefore blocks lines whose computation does not depend on it.

findings.situation: A filer received a Form 1099-INT that includes interest received as a nominee, has no foreign assets, and so truthfully answers NO; the tool then puts the full interest on line 2 without subtracting the nominee distribution.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p. 1: "Below this subtotal, enter 'Nominee Distribution' and show the total interest you received as a nominee. Subtract this amount from the subtotal and enter the result on line 2."
findings.why: Line 2 is the line 1 subtotal less nominee amounts, but the tool only adds interest entries. The Form 8938 question has nothing to do with nominee status, so this filer is never screened out.

findings.situation: A filer must subtract accrued interest paid on a bond purchase, an OID adjustment, or an amortizable bond premium adjustment, answers NO because they have no foreign assets, and the tool reports gross interest on line 2.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p. 2: "follow the rules earlier under Nominees to see how to report the accrued interest. But identify the amount to be subtracted as 'Accrued Interest.'" (similarly "OID Adjustment" and "ABP Adjustment")
findings.why: These subtractions reduce line 2 below the sum of interest entries. The tool does not make them, and a question about Form 8938 does not reach them.

findings.situation: A filer cashed post-1989 series EE or I savings bonds and paid qualified higher education expenses, answers NO because they have no foreign assets, and the tool sets line 3 to zero instead of the Form 8815 exclusion.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p. 2: "Line 3. If, during 2025, you cashed series EE or I U.S. savings bonds issued after 1989 and you paid qualified higher education expenses ... you may be able to exclude part or all of the interest on those bonds. See Form 8815"
findings.why: Line 3 is computed as a fixed zero, but the IRS text calls for a Form 8815 exclusion amount. Nothing in the Form 8938 question asks about savings bond redemptions or education expenses.

findings.situation: A filer received ordinary dividends as a nominee, answers NO because they have no foreign assets, and the tool enters the full Form 1099-DIV box 1a total on line 6.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p. 2: "Below this subtotal, enter 'Nominee Distribution' and show the total ordinary dividends you received as a nominee. Subtract this amount from the subtotal and enter the result on line 6."
findings.why: Line 6 must be reduced by nominee dividends, but the tool copies box 1a. The Form 8938 question does not identify nominee recipients.

findings.situation: A filer who is required to file Form 8938 must answer YES even though their interest and dividends are ordinary domestic amounts that the tool would put correctly on lines 2, 3 and 6.
findings.irs_text: Question: "Are you required to file Form 8938 for specified foreign financial assets?"; i1040sb p. 2: "Regardless of whether you are required to file FinCEN Form 114 (FBAR), you may be required to file Form 8938 ... with your income tax return."
findings.why: The Schedule B text treats Form 8938 only as a separate filing obligation. It does not change how lines 2, 3 or 6 are figured, so refusing these lines on a YES answer blocks amounts the tool computes correctly.

findings.situation: A filer with foreign accounts may not know whether they are "required" to file Form 8938, or may confuse that requirement with the FBAR or the line 7a foreign-account question.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p. 2: "Regardless of whether you are required to file FinCEN Form 114 (FBAR), you may be required to file Form 8938" (no thresholds or definition of "specified foreign financial assets" are given)
findings.why: The Schedule B instructions do not give the Form 8938 thresholds or define "specified foreign financial assets." A filer with foreign accounts could reasonably answer either way.

question: During 2025, did you receive a distribution from a foreign trust (a loan of cash or marketable securities counts), or were you the grantor of, or a transferor to, a foreign trust that existed at any time during 2025?

findings.situation: A filer was treated as the owner of a foreign trust under the grantor trust rules without being its grantor or a transferor to it, and received no distribution from it in 2025.
findings.irs_text: "If you were treated as the owner of a foreign trust under the grantor trust rules, you are also responsible for ensuring that the foreign trust files Form 3520-A." (i1040sb TY2025, p. 3, Line 8)
findings.why: The question asks only about distributions, grantors, and transferors, so this owner can truthfully answer NO. The tool then computes the lines and never raises the Form 3520-A responsibility that its refusal is meant to route.

findings.situation: A filer received a loan of cash or marketable securities from a foreign trust that falls outside the general rule and is not considered a distribution.
findings.irs_text: Question: "a loan of cash or marketable securities counts"; IRS: "a loan of cash or marketable securities is generally considered to be a distribution. See the Instructions for Form 3520" (i1040sb TY2025, p. 3, Line 8)
findings.why: The question turns the IRS's "generally" into an unconditional rule, so this filer must answer YES and is refused. The excepted loan does not change the computed lines, which the tool could otherwise handle correctly.

findings.situation: A grantor of, or transferor to, a foreign trust that existed during 2025 has no Form 3520 filing requirement for the year.
findings.irs_text: Question: "were you the grantor of, or a transferor to, a foreign trust that existed at any time during 2025?"; IRS: "If you were the grantor of, or transferor to, a foreign trust that existed during 2025, you may have to file Form 3520." (i1040sb TY2025, p. 3, Line 8)
findings.why: The IRS says only that such a filer "may" have to file, but the question requires YES whether or not a filing is due. The tool therefore refuses a filer with no Form 3520 obligation, even though the interest and dividend lines are unaffected.

findings.situation: A filer transferred property to a foreign trust before 2025, made no transfer during 2025, and the trust still existed during 2025.
findings.irs_text: "If you were the grantor of, or transferor to, a foreign trust that existed during 2025, you may have to file Form 3520." (i1040sb TY2025, p. 3, Line 8)
findings.why: The IRS text ties 2025 to the trust's existence, not to the transfer. The question's opening "During 2025" could be read to require that the filer acted as grantor or transferor in 2025, which would lead this filer to answer NO.

findings.why: The catch-all doesn't say what it includes. One filer could answer YES for items that don't affect lines 2, 3 or 6, while another answers NO for an item that does belong on line 1 and so in line 2.

question: Do you value closing inventory by a method other than cost or lower of cost or market, or was there any change in determining quantities, costs or valuations between opening and closing inventory (line 34)? Answer No if you have no inventory

findings.situation: A filer changing their inventory accounting method beginning with 2025 refigures last year's closing inventory under the new method, so opening and closing 2025 inventory are on the same basis and the filer can truthfully answer No if the new method is cost or lower of cost or market.
findings.irs_text: If you are changing your method of accounting beginning with 2025, refigure last year's closing inventory using your new method of accounting and enter the result on line 35. If there is a difference between last year's closing inventory and the refigured amount, attach an explanation and take it into account when figuring your section 481(a) adjustment. (i1040sc 2025 p. 15, Line 35)
findings.why: The question asks only about a change between opening and closing inventory, which misses a change between 2024 closing and 2025 opening inventory. The tool's input instructs the filer to enter the 2024 closing amount, rather than the refigured amount, and does not handle the explanation or section 481(a) adjustment.

findings.situation: A filer who consistently uses an IRS-approved method other than cost or lower of cost or market, with no change in method, must answer Yes even though line 35 is simply last year's closing inventory, which the tool's input takes correctly.
findings.irs_text: Question: "Do you value closing inventory by a method other than cost or lower of cost or market"; IRS: "Your inventories can be valued at cost, the lower of cost or market, or any other method approved by the IRS." (i1040sc 2025 p. 15, Line 33)
findings.why: The Line 35 text requires refiguring only when the method of accounting is changing, so consistent use of an approved other method does not make the entered amount wrong. For this line, the question refuses a case the tool computes correctly.

findings.situation: A small business taxpayer who chooses not to keep an inventory but holds unsold goods, or tracks them in books under a financial accounting method, could read "no inventory" as either no goods on hand or no formal inventory kept.
findings.irs_text: If you are a small business taxpayer, you can choose not to keep an inventory, but you must still use a method of accounting for inventory that clearly reflects income. (i1040sc 2025 p. 15, Part III, Exception for small business taxpayers)
findings.why: The wording does not say whether this filer should use the "Answer No" instruction. That choice can decide whether a filer whose treatment is neither cost nor lower of cost or market answers Yes and is refused, or answers No and has line 35 computed, possibly as zero.

findings.situation: A filer whose inventory counts or unit costs simply differ between the start and end of the year, with no change in method, could read "any change in determining quantities, costs or valuations" as covering those ordinary differences.
findings.irs_text: Question: "was there any change in determining quantities, costs or valuations between opening and closing inventory"; compare: "If you are changing your method of accounting beginning with 2025" (i1040sc 2025 p. 15, Line 35)
findings.why: The question means a change in how amounts are determined, but it does not use the words "method" or "accounting method". A filer could read it as covering ordinary changes in the amounts and wrongly answer Yes, even though the tool computes line 35 correctly.

findings.situation: A filer has income or loss from a passive activity reported on Schedule C, such as a sole-proprietor business they did not materially participate in. They answer NO because the question excludes Schedule C business income, so the tool sets eic.step2_other to false.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 40, EIC Step 2, question 4: "Do any of the following apply for 2025? ... • You have income or loss from a passive activity. Yes. Use Worksheet 1 ... in Pub. 596"
findings.why: Only the 'Schedule E or a Schedule K-1' item points to passive income, and the question tells the filer that Schedule C business income is asked about separately. A passive Schedule C activity therefore reaches a NO answer even though Step 2 question 4 requires Worksheet 1.

findings.situation: A sole proprietor on Schedule C, like the IRS's travel-guide example, received qualified tips in the business. They answer NO because Schedule C income is asked about separately, so the tool enters $0 for Schedule 1-A line 5.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 104, Schedule 1-A line 5: "Include the qualified tips you and/or your spouse received in the course of a trade or business, but only to the extent the trade or business ... has net income"; Example 2: "You enter $7,000 on Schedule 1-A, line 5."
findings.why: The question names Schedule E, K-1 and farm income but explicitly excludes Schedule C business income, which the tool computes. A Schedule C filer with tips answers NO, and the tool silently zeroes a deduction the IRS text allows.

findings.situation: A filer received qualified overtime reported on Form 1099-NEC box 1 and reports it on Schedule C. They answer NO because Schedule C business income is asked about separately, so Schedule 1-A line 14b is treated as $0.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 108, Line 14b: "Enter on Line 14b only the qualified overtime compensation amount that is included in Form 1099-NEC, box 1, or Form 1099-MISC, box 3."
findings.why: Nothing in the question's wording covers nonemployee compensation or 1099 overtime. The exclusion of Schedule C income actively steers this filer to NO.

findings.situation: A statutory employee reports W-2 box 13 wages on Schedule C and must decide whether the 'business income or loss from Schedule C' exclusion or the 'statutory-employee wages' item applies.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 42, Step 5 question 2: "...or are you filing Schedule C as a statutory employee?"; i1040s8812 p. 8, line 2a: "Enter any statutory employee income reported on line 1 of Schedule C"
findings.why: The question both lists statutory-employee wages as a YES item and tells the filer that Schedule C business income is asked separately. A statutory employee filing Schedule C could reasonably read either one as governing.

findings.situation: A filer had less than $108.28 of church employee wages and does not file Schedule SE. The question makes them answer YES, although the EIC worksheet line 1 simply uses Form 1040 line 1z, which the tool computes.
findings.irs_text: Question: "church employee income (wages from a church or qualified church-controlled organization that elected exemption ...)"; i1040gi p. 42, Step 5 question 1: "Are you filing Schedule SE because you were a member of the clergy or you had church employee income of $108.28 or more?"; i1040sse p. 1: "You must file Schedule SE if: ... You had church employee income of $108.28 or more."
findings.why: The IRS adjustment applies only when Schedule SE is filed, but the question has no $108.28 threshold. Every church employee is therefore refused.

findings.situation: A filer rents out personal property as part of a trade or business reported on Schedule C. They could read 'rental of personal property' as requiring YES, or treat it as Schedule C business income that is asked separately.
findings.irs_text: Question: "rental of personal property"; i1040gi p. 40, Step 2 question 4: "You are reporting income from the rental of personal property not used in a trade or business."
findings.why: The IRS item is limited to property not used in a trade or business, but the question drops that qualifier while also excluding Schedule C income. The two parts of the question point in opposite directions.

findings.situation: A filer born before January 2, 1961 has income high enough that the enhanced senior deduction phases out to zero, so Schedule 1-A line 38 is $0. The tool's $0 on line 13b would be correct, but the filer answers YES because of their birth date.
findings.irs_text: f1040 (2025) p.2, line 12d: "You: Were born before January 2, 1961"; line 13b: "Additional deductions from Schedule 1-A, line 38"
findings.why: The question names the deduction as "the enhanced deduction for a filer born before January 2, 1961," so birth date alone reads as qualifying. Any filer who checks the line 12d box would answer YES and be refused, even when the Schedule 1-A amount is zero. The income phase-out itself is not in the supplied text.

findings.situation: A filer received tips (line 1c or W-2) or overtime pay but does not know whether these count as "qualified tips" or "qualified overtime compensation."

findings.why: "Qualified" is a defined term that none of the supplied text explains, so a filer with tips or overtime could reasonably answer either way. If they answer NO when the items do qualify, line 13b becomes $0 and a deduction they are owed is missed.

question: Is there a capital loss carried into 2025 from any earlier year?

findings.situation: A filer with a short-term or long-term capital gain or loss passed through on a partnership, S corporation, estate, or trust Schedule K-1, but no prior-year capital loss, truthfully answers NO, and lines 5 and 12 are entered as zero.
findings.irs_text: 5 Net short-term gain or (loss) from partnerships, S corporations, estates, and trusts from Schedule(s) K-1 ... 12 Net long-term gain or (loss) from partnerships, S corporations, estates, and trusts from Schedule(s) K-1 (f1040sd 2025, p. 1)
findings.why: The question asks only about carryovers. Pass-through capital gain or loss is a separate source that the wording never mentions, so the tool treats it as zero without refusing.

findings.situation: A filer with an installment-sale gain (Form 6252), a casualty or theft gain or loss (Form 4684), a section 1256 or straddle result (Form 6781), a like-kind exchange (Form 8824), a Form 4797 Part I gain, or undistributed long-term gain (Form 2439) truthfully answers NO, and lines 4 and 11 are entered as zero.
findings.irs_text: 4 Short-term gain from Form 6252 and short-term gain or (loss) from Forms 4684, 6781, and 8824 ... 11 Gain from Form 4797, Part I; long-term gain from Forms 2439 and 6252; and long-term gain or (loss) from Forms 4684, 6781, and 8824 (f1040sd 2025, p. 1)
findings.why: None of these sources is a carryover from an earlier year, so a truthful NO zeroes lines 4 and 11. The line labels ('zero only after unsupported source/carryover screening') assume a source screen that this question does not perform.

findings.situation: A filer had a net capital loss on the 2024 Schedule D, or negative 2024 taxable income, but does not know whether any of the loss remains after the $3,000 deduction, so cannot tell whether a loss is 'carried into 2025'.
findings.irs_text: 6 Short-term capital loss carryover. Enter the amount, if any, from line 8 of your Capital Loss Carryover Worksheet in the instructions ... 14 Long-term capital loss carryover. Enter the amount, if any, from line 13 of your Capital Loss Carryover Worksheet (f1040sd 2025, p. 1)
findings.why: The carryover amount is the result of the worksheet, so 'is there a capital loss carried into 2025' can only be answered after the worksheet the tool declines to prepare. A filer whose prior loss may have been fully absorbed could reasonably answer either way.

question: Are there gains or losses from (or that belong on) Forms 4797, 2439, 6252, 4684, 6781 or 8824, or capital gains or losses on a Schedule K-1? Count section 1256 contracts and a casualty or theft of property whether you held the property directly or through an entity.

findings.situation: A filer whose only Form 4797 amount is a loss or a gain that is not a Part I gain (for example, ordinary gain from Part II) must answer YES, although nothing from that form reaches Schedule D and the zero on line 11 is correct.
findings.irs_text: Question: "Are there gains or losses from (or that belong on) Forms 4797..."; f1040sd (2025) p. 1, line 11: "Gain from Form 4797, Part I"
findings.why: Line 11 takes only gain from Form 4797, Part I, while the question counts any gain or loss on the form. The filer is refused on these Schedule D lines even though the tool's zero is correct for them.

findings.situation: A filer with a personal casualty or theft whose Form 4684 result is a loss that does not go to Schedule D, or that is not deductible, is told to count it and answers YES, although lines 4 and 11 are correctly zero.
findings.irs_text: Question: "Count section 1256 contracts and a casualty or theft of property whether you held the property directly or through an entity."; f1040sd (2025) p. 1, line 4: "short-term gain or (loss) from Forms 4684, 6781, and 8824"
findings.why: The lines take only amounts that Form 4684 sends to Schedule D, but the question counts a casualty or theft without that limit. The routing of personal casualty losses comes from Form 4684, which is not in the supplied text, so this rests on knowledge of that form.

findings.situation: A filer with a casualty or theft that produced no gain or loss, such as one fully reimbursed at basis, cannot tell whether the event itself counts or only a resulting gain or loss.
findings.irs_text: Question: "Count ... a casualty or theft of property"; f1040sd (2025) p. 1, line 11: "long-term gain or (loss) from Forms 4684, 6781, and 8824"
findings.why: The second sentence can be read as an instruction to count every such event, or only as clarifying what counts as a gain or loss under the first sentence. The first reading gives YES and the second gives NO, and with no amount for Schedule D the correct answer is NO.

findings.situation: A filer with a fully deferred like-kind exchange on Form 8824 has a realized gain but no recognized gain, and could read "gains" either way.
findings.irs_text: Question: "gains or losses from (or that belong on) Forms ... 8824"; f1040sd (2025) p. 1, line 11: "long-term gain or (loss) from Forms 4684, 6781, and 8824"
findings.why: The question does not say whether a deferred gain counts or only an amount the form carries to Schedule D. If nothing carries over, line 11 is correctly zero, but a filer could still answer YES because the deferred gain appears on the form.

findings.situation: A filer whose Schedule K-1 shows only net section 1231 gain might answer NO because the K-1 does not label it a capital gain, even if that gain belongs on Form 4797, Part I and reaches line 11.
findings.irs_text: Question: "or capital gains or losses on a Schedule K-1"; f1040sd (2025) p. 1, line 11: "Gain from Form 4797, Part I"
findings.why: The clause "or that belong on" Form 4797 technically requires YES, but the K-1 clause suggests that only items labeled capital count. A filer who does not know this routing could answer NO, and the tool would then wrongly treat line 11 as zero. The routing of K-1 section 1231 gain comes from text not supplied here.
